Cut the rod of length 5 into 5 rods of length (1, 1, 1, 1, 1) and sell them for (3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3) = 15.
Explanation 2:
Cut the rod of length 5 into 3 rods of length (2, 2, 1) and sell them for (5 + 5 + 1) = 11.
story: Partition a rod of length N into pieces to maximise total price, with every piece size reusable.
plain: A[i - 1] is the price of a piece of length i, and any piece size may be used any number of times. Define best(L) as the maximum revenue from a rod of remaining length L. For every possible first cut i from 1 to L, the revenue is A[i - 1] + best(L - i); take the maximum over all i. best(0) = 0 anchors the recursion. Memoise on L alone, so each of the N lengths is computed once with an O(L) inner scan, and return best(N).
howToThink: Unbounded knapsack: piece length is the weight, price is the value, capacity is `N`, and every piece size stays available forever.
State is a single integer — the remaining length. No `(index, length)` pair is needed because you never exhaust a piece size.
Transition: try every first cut `i` in `1..L`, pay `A[i - 1]`, recurse on `L - i`, keep the max.
`memory[L - 1]` stores the answer for length `L` — the shift exists only because the array is sized `N`, not `N + 1`.
Bottom-up equivalent: `dp[L] = max over i of (A[i - 1] + dp[L - i])`, sweeping `L` ascending.
pitfalls: Off-by-one on the price lookup: a piece of length `i` costs `A[i - 1]`, not `A[i]`.
Memo sentinel must be `-1`. `0` is a legitimate profit (length-0 rod), so a zero-filled memo returns stale zeros.
The `index == 0` base must return BEFORE any `memory[index - 1]` access, otherwise you index `-1`.
Max revenue reaches `1000 × 10^6 = 10^9`, which still fits `int` — but any extra accumulation on top of that needs `long`.

solutions.label: Optimal — memoised rod cutting on remaining length

complexity.space: O(N) — memo, plus O(N) call stack

solutions.plain: Fill a memo array of size N with -1. The recursion takes the remaining length index and returns 0 once it reaches 0. For each length, loop the first-cut size i from 1 to index, add the price A[i - 1] to the recursive result for index - i, and track the maximum. Cache under memory[index - 1] before returning. Every length is expanded once and each expansion is an O(N) scan, so the whole thing is O(N^2).
approach: Loop `i = 1 .. index`: `currentProfit = A[i - 1] + solve(index - i)`, keep the running max.
Store the max in `memory[index - 1]` and return it.
solutions.pseudocode:
solve(L):
    L == 0 → 0
    memory[L-1] != -1 → memory[L-1]
    best = 0
    for i = 1 .. L:
        best = max(best, A[i-1] + solve(L - i))
    memory[L-1] = best
    return best
solutions.story: Fix only the first cut; the rest of the rod is the same problem on a shorter length.

title: 0-1 Knapsack II
subTopic: 0/1 knapsack — capacity DP vs value DP
description:
Given two integer arrays A and B of size N each which represent values and weights associated with N items respectively.
Also given an integer C which represents knapsack capacity.
Find out the maximum value subset of A such that sum of the weights of this subset is smaller than or equal to C.
NOTE: You cannot break an item, either pick the complete item, or don't pick it (0-1 property).

Problem Constraints
1 <= N <= 500
1 <= C, B[i] <= 10^6
1 <= A[i] <= 50

Input Format
First argument is an integer array A of size N denoting the values on N items.
Second argument is an integer array B of size N denoting the weights on N items.
Third argument is an integer C denoting the knapsack capacity.

Output Format
Return a single integer denoting the maximum value subset of A such that sum of the weights of this subset is smaller than or equal to C.

Example Input
Input 1:
A = [6, 10, 12]
B = [10, 20, 30]
C = 50
Input 2:
A = [1, 3, 2, 4]
B = [12, 13, 15, 19]
C = 10

Example Output
Output 1:
22
Output 2:
0

Example Explanation
Explanation 1:
Taking items with weight 20 and 30 will give us the maximum value i.e 10 + 12 = 22
Explanation 2:
Knapsack capacity is 10 but each item has weight greater than 10 so no items can be considered in the knapsack therefore answer is 0.
story: Pick a subset of items whose weights fit the capacity and whose values sum to the maximum.
plain: Every item is pick-or-skip. Keep dp[w] = the best value achievable using capacity at most w with the items processed so far. For each item, sweep w from C down to B[i] and set dp[w] = max(dp[w], A[i] + dp[w - B[i]]). The descending sweep guarantees dp[w - B[i]] still holds the state before this item, which is what enforces at-most-one use. The answer is dp[C]. When capacity dwarfs the total value, flip the state: dp[v] = minimum total weight needed to reach value v, then report the largest v whose dp[v] is within C.
howToThink: 0/1 knapsack — pick-or-skip recursion on `(index, capacity)`, rolled down to a 1D array swept descending.
Descending `w` is the only thing that makes it 0/1; ascending `w` is the unbounded variant.
Read the constraints: `C <= 10^6` but `A[i] <= 50` and `N <= 500`, so total value never exceeds 25000 — the value axis is two orders of magnitude smaller than the capacity axis.
Value-DP state: `dp[v] = min weight to achieve exactly value v`; the answer is the largest `v` with `dp[v] <= C`.
Pick whichever axis is smaller — the pattern is the same, only the dimension you index by changes.
pitfalls: Ascending `w` in the 1D capacity DP reuses the same item multiple times — it silently becomes unbounded knapsack.
`int[] dp = new int[C + 1]` with `C = 10^6` is 4 MB and `O(N·C) = 5 × 10^8` transitions; workable but at the edge.
The value DP needs an INF sentinel for unreachable values — guard `dp[v - A[i]] != INF` before adding, otherwise the weight sum overflows.
`0` is a legal answer (Example 2: every weight exceeds `C`); don't special-case it into `-1` or an exception.

solutions.label: Optimal — 1D capacity knapsack, descending sweep
solutions.plain: Allocate dp over capacities 0..C, all zeros. For each item in turn, walk w downward from C to B[i] and relax dp[w] against A[i] + dp[w - B[i]]. Going downward means dp[w - B[i]] has not yet been touched by the current item, so each item enters at most one time. After all items, dp[C] is the answer; unreachable cases naturally stay at 0.
approach: Allocate `dp` of length `C + 1`, all zero — zero value is always achievable.
solutions.pseudocode:
dp[0..C] = 0
for i = 0 .. n-1:
    for w = C down to weights[i]:      # descending → item used at most once
        dp[w] = max(dp[w], values[i] + dp[w - weights[i]])
return dp[C]
solutions.story: Sweeping capacity backwards is the whole trick that keeps a 1D array honest about the 0/1 rule.

solutions.label: Alternative — min-weight-per-value DP (better when C is huge)
solutions.plain: Index the DP by value instead of capacity, because sum(A) is at most 500 * 50 = 25000 while C can be 10^6. dp[v] is the minimum total weight needed to reach value exactly v, initialised to INF except dp[0] = 0. For each item, sweep v downward and relax dp[v] against dp[v - A[i]] + B[i]. Finally scan v from the top and return the first value whose minimum weight is within C.
approach: Compute `totalValue = sum(A)` — at most 25000 under these constraints.
Allocate `long[] dp` of length `totalValue + 1`, fill with INF, set `dp[0] = 0`.
For each item, sweep `v` from `totalValue` down to `A[i]`.
If `dp[v - A[i]]` is reachable, relax `dp[v] = min(dp[v], dp[v - A[i]] + B[i])`.
Scan `v` from `totalValue` down to 0 and return the first `v` with `dp[v] <= C`.
solutions.story: When one axis is 10^6 and the other is 25000, index by the small one.

title: Distinct Subsequences
description:
Given two strings A and B, count the number of unique ways in string A to form a subsequence that is identical to string B.

A subsequence of a string is a new string formed from the original string by deleting some (can be none) of the characters without disturbing the relative positions of the remaining characters. (ie, "ACE" is a subsequence of "ABCDE" while "AEC" is not).

Since the answer can be very large, return the result modulo 10^9 + 7.

Problem Constraints
1 <= |A|, |B| <= 1000

Input Format
The first argument is a string A.
The second argument is a string B.

Output Format
Return an integer representing the number of distinct subsequences of A which equal B, modulo 10^9 + 7.

Example Input
Input 1:
A = "abc"
B = "abc"
Input 2:
A = "rabbbit"
B = "rabbit"

Example Output
Output 1:
1
Output 2:
3

Example Explanation
Explanation 1:
    Both strings are equal. There is exactly 1 way to form "abc"
    as a subsequence of "abc" - take all characters.

    Result: 1
Explanation 2:
    The string A = "rabbbit" has 3 'b' characters.
    To form B = "rabbit", we need exactly 2 'b' characters.
    We can remove any one of the 3 'b' characters:

    1. "ra_bbit" (remove 1st 'b')
    2. "rab_bit" (remove 2nd 'b')
    3. "rabb_it" (remove 3rd 'b')

    "_" marks the removed character.
story: Count how many index sets of A spell out B in order.
plain: Let dp[i][j] be the number of ways to form the first j characters of B out of the first i characters of A. Skipping A[i-1] always carries over dp[i-1][j]. If A[i-1] equals B[j-1] you may additionally consume it, adding dp[i-1][j-1]. The base is dp[i][0] = 1 for every i, since the empty prefix of B is formed exactly one way, and dp[0][j] = 0 for j > 0. Roll the table down to a single array over j and sweep j from m down to 1, so dp[j-1] still carries the previous row while you write dp[j]. The answer is dp[m] taken modulo 10^9 + 7.
howToThink: 2D subsequence-count DP over `(prefix of A, prefix of B)` — the LCS/edit-distance skeleton, but you SUM the branches instead of maxing them.
At `A[i-1]`: skipping is always available; matching is available only when `A[i-1] == B[j-1]`. Add the two counts.
Base row: `dp[i][0] = 1` (one way to form the empty string), `dp[0][j] = 0` for `j > 0`.
Rolling to 1D requires the inner loop to run `j = m .. 1` so `dp[j - 1]` is still row `i - 1`.
Only the 'equal characters' case writes anything — the skip branch is already sitting in `dp[j]` from the previous row.
pitfalls: Ascending inner `j` in the 1D version reads a `dp[j - 1]` that this same row already updated, double-counting one character of `A`.
Forgetting `% 1_000_000_007` — with `|A| = 1000` the counts blow past `int` fast.
The base must be `dp[0] = 1`, not `0`; seeding it to 0 zeroes the entire table.
This problem's modulus is `10^9 + 7`, unlike Coin Sum Infinite in the same set which uses `10^6 + 7`.

solutions.label: Optimal — 1D rolling subsequence-count DP
solutions.plain: Keep one array dp of length m + 1 with dp[0] = 1. Walk i through A. For each i, walk j from m down to 1, and whenever A[i-1] matches B[j-1], add dp[j-1] into dp[j] under the modulus. The descending j guarantees dp[j-1] is still the value from the previous character of A. After the outer loop dp[m] holds the count.
approach: Let `n = A.length()`, `m = B.length()`; allocate `dp` of length `m + 1`.
Set `dp[0] = 1` — one way to form the empty prefix of `B`.
Outer loop `i = 1 .. n` over characters of `A`.
solutions.story: Each character of A either contributes nothing or forks every partial match that was waiting for it.

title: Let's Party
description:
In Danceland, one person can party either alone or can pair up with another person.
Can you find in how many ways they can party if there are A people in Danceland?
Note: Return your answer modulo 10003, as the answer can be large.

Problem Constraints
1 <= A <= 10^5

Input Format
Given only argument A of type Integer, number of people in Danceland.

Output Format
Return an integer denoting the number of ways people of Danceland can party.

Example Input
Input 1:
A = 3
Input 2:
A = 5

Example Output
Output 1:
4
Output 2:
26

Example Explanation
Explanation 1:
Let suppose three people are A, B, and C. There are only 4 ways to party
(A, B, C) All party alone
(AB, C) A and B party together and C party alone
(AC, B) A and C party together and B party alone
(BC, A) B and C party together and A
here 4 % 10003 = 4, so answer is 4.
Explanation 2:
Number of ways they can party are: 26.
story: Count the ways to split A people into singles and unordered pairs.
plain: Fix attention on the last person, number i. Either they party alone, which leaves the remaining i - 1 people to arrange in f(i - 1) ways, or they pair with exactly one of the other i - 1 people, and after removing both you are left with f(i - 2) ways. That gives f(i) = f(i - 1) + (i - 1) * f(i - 2), anchored at f(0) = 1 and f(1) = 1. Iterate i from 2 to A carrying only the last two values, reducing by 10003 at each step, and return the final value.
howToThink: Linear recurrence `f(i) = f(i-1) + (i-1) * f(i-2)` — fix one person and split on alone versus paired.
The `(i - 1)` factor is the number of partner choices; once paired, BOTH leave, hence `f(i - 2)`.
Bases: `f(0) = 1` (empty set has one arrangement) and `f(1) = 1`.
Only the two previous values matter, so keep two scalars — no `O(A)` array needed.
pitfalls: `(i - 1) * f(i - 2)` overflows `int` before the mod when `i` approaches `10^5` — promote to `long` first, then reduce.
The modulus is `10003` (not `10^9 + 7`); apply it at every step, never once at the end.
`A = 1` must return 1 — the loop body never executes, so the seeds themselves must already be right.
Don't multiply by `i` instead of `i - 1`; the chosen person cannot pair with themselves, and a pair is unordered.

solutions.label: Optimal — O(1)-space linear recurrence
solutions.plain: Seed prev = f(0) = 1 and curr = f(1) = 1. Loop i from 2 to A computing next = curr + (i - 1) * prev, all in long, reduced modulo 10003. Shift prev to curr and curr to next each iteration. When A is 1 the loop never runs and curr is already the right answer. Return curr cast back to int.
solutions.pseudocode:
prev = 1            # f(0)
curr = 1            # f(1)
for i = 2 .. A:
    next = (curr + (i-1) * prev) % 10003
    prev = curr
    curr = next
return curr
solutions.story: One person decides alone-or-paired; the rest of the crowd is the same problem, one or two smaller.

title: Length of Longest Fibonacci Subsequence
subTopic: Pair-state DP on a sorted array
description:
Given a strictly increasing array A of positive integers forming a sequence.
A sequence X1, X2, X3, ..., XN is fibonacci like if
N > =3
Xi + Xi+1 = Xi+2 for all i+2 <= N
Find and return the length of the longest Fibonacci-like subsequence of A.
If one does not exist, return 0.
NOTE: A subsequence is derived from another sequence A by deleting any number of elements (including none) from A, without changing the order of the remaining elements.

Problem Constraints
3 <= length of the array <= 1000
1 <= A[i] <= 10^9

Input Format
The only argument given is the integer array A.

Output Format
Return the length of the longest Fibonacci-like subsequence of A.
If one does not exist, return 0.

Example Input
Input 1:
A = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]
Input 2:
A = [1, 3, 7, 11, 12, 14, 18]

Example Output
Output 1:
5
Output 2:
3

Example Explanation
Explanation 1:
The longest subsequence that is fibonacci-like: [1, 2, 3, 5, 8].
Explanation 2:
The longest subsequence that is fibonacci-like: [1, 11, 12], [3, 11, 14] or [7, 11, 18].
The length will be 3.
story: Find the longest subsequence where every term is the sum of the two before it.
plain: A Fibonacci-like chain is completely determined by its last two elements, so make the DP state a pair of indices. Let dp[j][k] be the length of the longest such subsequence whose final two terms are A[j] and A[k]. For a fixed pair, the required predecessor value is forced to be A[k] - A[j], and because A is strictly increasing that predecessor must be strictly smaller than A[j], so you binary search for it inside A[0..j-1]. If it is found at index i, then dp[j][k] is dp[i][j] + 1 when (i, j) already extends a chain, and 3 otherwise since you have just the three terms. Track the running maximum and return 0 if nothing ever reaches length 3.
howToThink: Pair-state DP: `dp[j][k]` keyed on the LAST TWO elements — one index is not enough because the next term depends on two.
Given `A[j]` and `A[k]`, the predecessor value is forced: `A[k] - A[j]`. You look it up, you never search over it.
`A` is strictly increasing, so the predecessor must satisfy `A[k] - A[j] < A[j]` — that prunes half the pairs and makes binary search valid.
`dp[i][j] == 0` means `(i, j)` is not yet part of any chain, so the new chain length is exactly 3, not 2 + 1.
Swap the binary search for a value→index hash map and it drops to `O(N^2)` time.
pitfalls: Returning 2. Anything shorter than 3 is not Fibonacci-like, so the base jump is straight to 3 and the default answer stays 0.
Skipping the `A[k] - A[j] < A[j]` guard lets you match an index `i >= j` and build a bogus non-increasing chain.
`A[i] <= 10^9`, so a forward formulation that computes `A[j] + A[k]` overflows `int`; the backward `A[k] - A[j]` lookup sidesteps it entirely.
`dp` is `N × N` = 10^6 ints at `N = 1000` — fine once, but never reallocate it inside the outer loop.

solutions.label: Optimal — pair-state DP with binary-searched predecessor
solutions.plain: Allocate an N by N table of zeros. Iterate k from 2 upward and j from 1 to k - 1, treating (A[j], A[k]) as the final pair. Compute target = A[k] - A[j] and skip immediately if it is not strictly less than A[j], since the array is strictly increasing. Otherwise binary search target inside A[0..j-1]; if index i is found, set dp[j][k] to dp[i][j] + 1 when dp[i][j] is non-zero and to 3 otherwise. Keep the running maximum and return it, which is 0 when no triple exists.
approach: Outer loop `k = 2 .. n - 1`, inner loop `j = 1 .. k - 1`.
`target = A[k] - A[j]`; if `target >= A[j]`, skip — no valid earlier index can hold it.
Binary search `target` in `A[0 .. j - 1]`; skip if absent.
solutions.pseudocode:
dp[n][n] = 0; best = 0
for k = 2 .. n-1:
    for j = 1 .. k-1:
        target = A[k] - A[j]
        if target >= A[j] → skip        # strictly increasing ⇒ predecessor < A[j]
        i = binarySearch(A, target, 0, j-1)
        if i < 0 → skip
        dp[j][k] = (dp[i][j] == 0) ? 3 : dp[i][j] + 1
        best = max(best, dp[j][k])
return best
solutions.story: The last two terms pin the whole chain, so the state is a pair and the predecessor is arithmetic, not search.

title: Ways to Decode
description:
A message containing letters from A-Z is being encoded to numbers using the following mapping:

'A' -> 1
'B' -> 2
...
'Z' -> 26

Given an encoded message denoted by string A containing digits, determine the total number of ways to decode it modulo 10^9 + 7.

Problem Constraints
1 <= length(A) <= 10^5

Input Format
The first and the only argument is a string A.

Output Format
Return an integer, representing the number of ways to decode the string modulo 10^9 + 7.

Example Input
Input 1:
A = "12"
Input 2:
A = "8"

Example Output
Output 1:
2
Output 2:
1

Example Explanation
Explanation 1:
Given encoded message "12", it could be decoded as "AB" (1, 2) or "L" (12).
The number of ways decoding "12" is 2.
Explanation 2:
Given encoded message "8", it could be decoded as only "H" (8).
The number of ways decoding "8" is 1.
story: Each position either consumes one digit or two, giving a Fibonacci-shaped recurrence with validity guards.
plain: Let dp[i] be the number of decodings of the first i characters. To extend to position i you either take A[i-1] alone, which is legal when that digit is not '0', contributing dp[i-1]; or you take A[i-2..i-1] as a two-digit letter, which is legal when that pair reads between 10 and 26, contributing dp[i-2]. Sum the legal options mod 1e9+7. dp[0] = 1 (the empty prefix has one decoding) and dp[1] = 1 provided the first character is not '0'. Only the last two values are ever needed, so roll them in two variables.
howToThink: Linear DP on prefixes: `dp[i] = dp[i-1] (if single digit valid) + dp[i-2] (if the two-digit pair is 10..26)`.
Every decoding is a sequence of 1-digit and 2-digit cuts, so the count only depends on the two previous prefix counts - that is the Fibonacci skeleton.
'0' is the whole difficulty: it can never stand alone, and it is only decodable as the tail of "10" or "20".
The pair guard must be `10 <= two <= 26`, not `two <= 26` - "06" is not a valid 'F'.
Since only `dp[i-1]` and `dp[i-2]` matter, drop the array and keep `prev1` / `prev2`.
pitfalls: Allowing a leading-zero pair like "06" by testing only `two <= 26`.
Returning 1 for a string starting with '0' - it has zero decodings, so bail out immediately.
Forgetting `% MOD` - with length up to 1e5 the count overflows int long before the end.
Setting `dp[0] = 0`; the empty prefix must be 1 or the two-digit branch never contributes.

solutions.label: Optimal - rolling two-variable DP
solutions.plain: Reject immediately if the string is empty or begins with '0'. Initialise prev2 = 1 for the empty prefix and prev1 = 1 for the first character. Walk i from 2 to N, adding prev1 when A[i-1] is a non-zero digit and adding prev2 when the two characters ending at i form a number in [10, 26]. Reduce mod 1e9+7 at every step and shift the two counters forward. prev1 holds the answer at the end.
approach: Compute `two` from characters `i-2` and `i-1`; if `10 <= two <= 26`, add `prev2` and take `% MOD`.
solutions.pseudocode:
A empty or A[0] == '0' -> return 0

prev2 = 1     // dp[0], empty prefix
prev1 = 1     // dp[1]

for i = 2 .. n:
    curr = 0
    A[i-1] != '0'        -> curr += prev1
    two = A[i-2]*10 + A[i-1]
    10 <= two <= 26      -> curr += prev2
    curr %= MOD
    prev2 = prev1
    prev1 = curr

return prev1
solutions.story: Count cuts, not letters: each step is a Fibonacci sum gated by two validity checks.

title: Flip Array
description:
Given an array A of positive elements, you have to flip the sign of some of its elements such that the resultant sum of the elements of array should be minimum non-negative(as close to zero as possible).
Return the minimum number of elements whose sign needs to be flipped such that the resultant sum is minimum non-negative.

Problem Constraints
1 <= length of(A) <= 100
Sum of all the elements will not exceed 10,000.

Input Format
First and only argument is an integer array A.

Output Format
Return an integer denoting the minimum number of elements whose sign needs to be flipped.

Example Input
Input 1:
A = [15, 10, 6]
Input 2:
A = [14, 10, 4]

Example Output
Output 1:
1
Output 2:
1

Example Explanation
Explanation 1:
Here, we will flip the sign of 15 and the resultant sum will be 1.
Explanation 2:
Here, we will flip the sign of 14 and the resultant sum will be 0.
Note that flipping the sign of 10 and 4 also gives the resultant sum 0 but flippings there sign are not minimum.
story: Flipping a subset S makes the sum total - 2*sum(S), so maximise sum(S) under total/2 with fewest elements.
plain: If you flip the subset S, the resultant sum is total - 2*sum(S). Keeping it non-negative means sum(S) <= total/2, and making it minimal means pushing sum(S) as high as possible under that cap. So run a 0/1 knapsack over sums 0..total/2 where dp[s] is the minimum number of elements needed to hit exactly s, initialised to infinity except dp[0] = 0. Process each element once, iterating s downward so each element is used at most once. Then scan s from total/2 downward and return the first dp[s] that is reachable.
howToThink: 0/1 subset-sum knapsack on the flipped set: `dp[s]` = fewest elements summing to exactly `s`, capped at `total / 2`.
Do the algebra first - flipping subset `S` gives `total - 2*sum(S)`, which reframes the whole problem as "get `sum(S)` as close to `total/2` from below".
The cap comes straight from the constraint `Sum <= 10000`, so the DP table is at most 5001 wide and `O(N * sum)` is fine.
Two objectives stacked: first maximise `s`, then minimise the count at that `s` - scanning `s` downward and returning the first reachable `dp[s]` handles both.
Iterate `s` from `half` down to `value` so each element is consumed once (classic 0/1 direction).
pitfalls: Iterating `s` upward, which turns it into unbounded knapsack and reuses an element many times.
Minimising `|total - 2s|` over all `s` instead of restricting to `s <= total / 2` - the result must be non-negative.
`Integer.MAX_VALUE` as the sentinel then doing `dp[s - value] + 1` without a reachability guard - that overflows to a negative count.
Forgetting `dp[0] = 0`, which leaves the whole table unreachable.
Using integer `total / 2` is correct here, but do not then compare against `total / 2.0` anywhere.

solutions.label: Optimal - 0/1 knapsack on subset sums, minimising count
solutions.plain: Compute total and half = total / 2. Build dp over 0..half with Integer.MAX_VALUE everywhere except dp[0] = 0. For each element, sweep s from half down to the element's value and relax dp[s] = min(dp[s], dp[s - value] + 1), skipping unreachable sources. Finally walk s from half downward and return the first dp[s] that is not the sentinel - that is the largest achievable subset sum under the cap, with the fewest elements.
approach: Sum the array into `total`; set `half = total / 2`.
For each `value` in A, loop `s` from `half` down to `value`.
If `dp[s - value]` is reachable, relax `dp[s] = min(dp[s], dp[s - value] + 1)`.
Scan `s` from `half` down to 0 and return the first reachable `dp[s]`.
